strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized, and the two-view framing (global layer-wise SVD plus token-level spectral analysis) is a nice conceptual device for thinking about feature-map KD in ViTs.

The proposed remedies (post-hoc linear projector retained at inference; widening only the last block) are simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to implement, and they do yield consistent accuracy improvements on ImageNet-1K across several teachers (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small).

The authors honestly report that the architectural modifications improve the student even without any teacher (Table 7, +0.55/+0.68), which is a genuinely interesting additional finding and is not hidden.
Experiments follow the standard DeiT recipe on ImageNet-1K with 300-epoch training, and the ablation set (heads, projector width, loss weight) is reasonable in scope.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method "reactivates" feature-map KD is not cleanly supported because of a serious confound: the architectural changes themselves improve the student (Table 7: +0.55 for Strategy 1, +0.68 for Strategy 2 standalone), and logit KD already accounts for most of the headline gains (e.g., Strategy 2 with SoftKD alone = 77.88 vs 78.23 with MSE). The marginal contribution of feature KD on top of logit KD is only ~+0.27 (Strategy 1) and ~+0.35 (Strategy 2), which is small and, with no seeds or error bars reported, plausibly within run-to-run noise. The headline framing "74.86% to 77.53%/78.23%" conflates the architecture change, logit KD, and feature KD.

The token-level SEP diagnostic is questionable. The DFT magnitude spectrum of a generic dense high-dimensional vector is approximately flat, so a near-diagonal cumulative-energy curve is the default behavior, not evidence of a ViT-specific "high-bandwidth encoding." The authors themselves acknowledge the channel axis has no intrinsic frequency meaning. As a result, SEP likely measures a generic property of unstructured vectors and does not establish the claimed ViT-specific "encoding mismatch."

The theoretical story does not cleanly explain Strategy 1: a linear projector from 192 to 384 is rank-192 and cannot increase the rank / "per-token encoding capacity" of the representation in the sense the paper claims. Thus the mechanism attributed to the projector's success (supplying missing per-token capacity) is not consistent with what a linear map can do, undermining the explanatory link between the analysis and the method.

The "paradox" motivating the paper is arguably not a paradox, and the analysis-to-method link is loose: the low-rank SVD already implies a modest bottleneck plus linear projector should suffice, which is essentially what Strategy 1 does, so it is unclear what new mechanism the SEP analysis contributes.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to strong ViT feature-distillation baselines (e.g., ViTKD, VKD, MiniViT, manifold distillation). The paper's only "naive feature KD" baseline is SpectralKD, which gives a very weak +0.21, so it is not established that the proposed methods are competitive with the state of the art; the claim that feature KD "fails" for ViTs is not well contextualized against methods that reportedly work.

Several ablations are over-interpreted given their magnitude: Table 4 differences (e.g., 75.46/75.53/75.41/75.23 across projector widths) are ~0.1-0.3% and show no clean trend, yet are used to argue for "matching the teacher's subspace." Without multiple seeds or variance estimates these interpretations are not warranted.

Reproducibility and rigor are limited: no seed variance or confidence intervals are reported for any result, no code/artifact release is mentioned, and there is no limitations discussion addressing the confounds above or the arbitrariness of the DFT-based diagnostic.

strengths: The paper conducts a broad, descriptive SVD characterization of final-layer representations across many architectures (Table 1; Appendix Figs. 3-7: ViT-Tiny/Small/Large/Huge, CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, Swin-Small), showing that last-layer features are consistently low-rank relative to channel width. This is a potentially useful empirical observation for compact-ViT design.
The idea of pairing a global (SVD) diagnostic with a token-level (SEP) diagnostic is conceptually appealing and the paper is clearly organized around it.

The proposed interventions are simple, architecture-agnostic, and easy to reproduce; the training recipe (300 epochs, AdamW, batch 2048, loss weights) is described in enough detail to be reimplemented.
The paper reports standalone (teacher-free) results and an ablation over projector width/head type, which are the right kinds of controls to attempt.
weaknesses: The central 'paradox' motivating the paper rests on a flawed use of Eckart-Young-Mirsky. The low-rank argument constructs an oracle bottleneck Z (the top-d left singular vectors/scores of the teacher itself) and shows it can be linearly mapped back to X_T. This says nothing about whether a narrow *student network* can produce that code. Low-rankness of the teacher's output does not imply that a shared linear projector can align a student, so the 'low-rank yet hard to distill' paradox is not a genuine contradiction. The whole narrative is built on this non-sequitur.

The SEP analysis is computed with a 1D DFT along the channel index, an arbitrary basis unrelated to the SVD subspace. A near-diagonal cumulative spectrum simply means the channel-wise signal has an approximately flat (white-noise-like) power spectrum, which is the generic case for non-smooth signals and does not constitute evidence of meaningful 'high per-token utilization' or 'channel bandwidth.' Consequently, the claimed 'two sides of the same coin' resolution is not established: SVD and SEP live in different bases and are not complementary in the way asserted.

Results are marginal and lack statistical rigor. There are single runs, no seeds, and no error bars anywhere. Several claimed gains (74.86 -> 75.07; 75.41 vs 75.54; standalone +0.55/+0.68) fall within typical ImageNet run-to-run variance. Critically, the feature-KD 'reactivation' adds only ~0.3-0.7% over logit KD alone (Strategy 2: 77.88 SoftKD-only vs 78.23 SoftKD+MSE; 78.16 SoftKD+SpectralKD). The headline 78.23% is therefore driven mostly by logit distillation, not by the feature-KD mechanism the paper claims to fix.

No control for added capacity/parameters. Both strategies add parameters (a D_S x D_T projector retained at inference, or a widened final block). The gains may simply reflect increased model capacity rather than 'matching the teacher's subspace.' The projector-dimension ablation (256/320/384/448) shows non-monotonic differences of ~0.1% (75.23-75.53), which is too noisy to support the strong 'match the teacher, not blindly increase dimensionality' conclusion.

Weak baselines and missing comparisons. The premise that 'naive feature KD fails for ViTs' is supported by a single method (SpectralKD, +0.21%). This conflicts with prior work (e.g., ViTKD) that reports substantial feature-KD gains for ViTs. The paper does not compare against strong feature-KD baselines (ViTKD, ReviewKD, etc.), so the claim that the proposed remedies 'reactivate' feature KD is not convincingly situated against the state of the art.

Internal inconsistency about the mechanism. If per-token encoding truly required high bandwidth, earlier layers (kept at D_S) would also be bottlenecked, yet only widening the last block helps. Moreover, Strategy 1 (a purely linear post-hoc projector) fixes the problem, which directly contradicts the claim that the student 'lacks the representational capacity' to realize the teacher's encoding. The mechanism as described does not uniquely predict the observed fix.

Presentation issues: Table 2 mixes strategy and KD method in confusing rows; notation is inconsistent (Eq. 2 uses l while the text defines r); the abstract lists ranks in an order (121/61/34/14) that is easy to misread against the stated energy levels.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and clearly motivated question: why feature-map knowledge distillation, which is effective for CNNs, often fails for Vision Transformers.
It proposes a two-view representation analysis (global SVD and token-level SEP) that, despite flaws, offers an interpretable perspective and a testable hypothesis about width/encoding mismatch.
The two proposed remedies are simple and architecture-agnostic: a lightweight post-hoc projector retained at inference and widening only the final Transformer block.
Experiments are conducted on ImageNet-1K with multiple teachers (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small) and include ablations on classifier head, projector dimension, and feature-loss weight.
The standalone gains without any teacher (+0.55/+0.68 for DeiT-Tiny) provide some support that last-layer width is an architectural bottleneck.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, and the main empirical trends are easy to follow.
weaknesses: The SEP analysis applies a 1D DFT along the channel dimension, but ViT channels have no natural frequency ordering and are permutation-dependent. The nearly diagonal cumulative energy curve is expected for generic non-sparse vectors and does not by itself establish 'high per-token utilization' or an encoding mismatch; a null/random baseline or permutation control is missing.

The global low-rank claim is confounded by token count: for a feature matrix X in R^{N x D}, the rank is at most N (e.g., 197 tokens). CaiT-S24's 99th-percentile 99%-energy rank of 121 is not as dramatically low relative to the maximum possible rank as the paper implies. The abstract also mixes 99th-percentile values (121/61/34/14) with typical values (mean 99%-energy rank is 84.6).

The central 'encoding mismatch' theory is not logically coherent: if the teacher's features are globally low-rank (e.g., 121 dimensions for 99% energy), a 192-dimensional student already has enough rank in principle to represent them; a linear projector cannot increase the student's rank or intrinsic capacity beyond its width. The success of Strategy 1 is more simply explained by a wider classifier head plus logit KD, not by resolving a fundamental capacity mismatch.

Feature-KD gains are modest and confounded with architectural and logit-KD gains. Strategy 1 with SoftKD alone reaches 77.23%, while adding MSE/SpectralKD gives only +0.27/+0.30; Strategy 2 with SoftKD alone reaches 77.88%, adding MSE gives +0.35. The largest improvements over the 74.86% baseline come from the projector/head change and logit distillation, not from feature-map KD itself.

The paper does not compare against strong ViT KD baselines (e.g., DeiT's distillation token, ViTKD, ReviewKD, VKD) or against simply widening the student/head without feature KD, making it difficult to assess the practical significance of the proposed 'reactivation'.

Generality across teachers is mixed: with DeiT-Small, Strategy 1 MSE reaches 76.22% while Strategy 2 SpectralKD reaches 75.73%, and no SoftKD+feature-KD results are reported for these teachers. The pattern is less consistent than the CaiT-S24 results suggest.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release, no multiple seeds or error bars, and no detailed hyperparameter search. ImageNet results are single-run and may be noisy, especially for the small deltas claimed.

Limitations and failure cases are not discussed. There is no analysis of the inference overhead and parameter counts of the modified models, no discussion of when the proposed remedies may fail, and no ethics/limitations section.
Some notation and presentation issues remain: Eq. (2) uses l rather than the defined r; Table 1's 'Last Feature' column is unclear; and the paper sometimes conflates mean and 99th-percentile ranks.

The claim of 'reactivating simple feature-map KD' is weakened by the fact that the best feature-KD variant is often SpectralKD, which is not a simple MSE feature loss, and MSE-only feature KD remains below logit-only KD in several settings.

strengths: The paper asks a genuinely interesting and practically relevant question: why feature-map KD is unreliable in wide-to-narrow ViT compression, and the framing (per-image low-rank vs. dataset-level non-low-rank) is a clean and intuitive way to set up the problem.

The SVD vs. shared-PCA diagnostic (Section 2.4, Figure 1, Table 1) is coherently executed and shows the subspace-rotation phenomenon across a broad range of architectures and training regimes (SL/SSL/MM), which is a useful empirical characterization.

The two proposed remedies are simple, easy to implement, and the paper reports consistent empirical improvements, including standalone (no-teacher) gains (Table 7), which is a nontrivial and interesting observation.
The manuscript is generally well-written, the narrative is clear, and the training protocol is described in enough detail to be plausibly reproducible; code/raw data are promised in the supplement.

The ablation studies (head type, projector width, feature-loss weight) are sensible and the projector-width ablation showing that matching the teacher width is preferable to blindly increasing width is a reasonable sanity check.
weaknesses: The central SEP analysis is essentially a null result dressed up as a discovery. A 1D DFT along the channel axis of a generic high-dimensional vector yields a near-flat power spectrum, so the cumulative spectral energy is approximately diagonal for almost any non-degenerate feature vector (including random noise). Observing '~50% energy in ~50% bins, ~90% in ~90% bins' therefore does not establish an 'architecture-invariant encoding law' or 'spectral universality'; it merely says the token vectors are not sparse in the Fourier basis. No control (e.g., random Gaussian vectors, shuffled channels, or a non-ViT baseline) is provided to show the curve differs from a trivial baseline. This undermines contribution #2 and, consequently, the proposed 'bandwidth mismatch' mechanism.

The causal link between the 'encoding mismatch' diagnosis and the fixes is not established. Lift is a retained linear projector (an extra linear layer / wider classifier interface) and WideLast simply widens the last block. Both add endpoint capacity/parameters. The paper never rules out the alternative explanation that the gains come from added capacity/parameters or better optimization rather than from resolving a specific 'encoding mismatch.' No mechanism-isolating control experiment is presented (e.g., adding a parameter-matched projection elsewhere, or matching capacity without width alignment).

The main results are heavily confounded with logit distillation. In Table 2, Lift+SoftKD alone already yields +2.37 over baseline, and the standalone Lift/WideLast gains are +0.55/+0.68. Thus a large fraction of the headline improvement comes from logit KD and added capacity, not from 'reactivating feature KD.' The feature-KD-specific gain (e.g., MSE going from ineffective to +1.75) is real but the framing overstates the role of the proposed diagnosis in the overall accuracy improvements.

The empirical comparison is too narrow to support the strong claim that feature KD is 'revived.' Only SpectralKD is used to represent 'naive feature KD,' and there is no comparison against established ViT feature-KD methods (e.g., ViTKD, ScaleKD, VkD, OFA-KD) under matched conditions, so the reader cannot judge whether the proposed fixes are competitive or merely add capacity.

Generality is limited: the primary study uses a single teacher-student pair (CaiT-S24 → DeiT-Tiny), and the 'generality across teachers' experiments (Table 6) are thin, showing smaller and mixed gains. The claim that the diagnosis 'can be applied across multiple ViT-family teachers whenever the last-layer width mismatch exists' is not strongly supported.

The standalone gains (+0.55, +0.68) are small and reported for a single run; no multiple seeds or variance estimates are given, so it is unclear whether these are within typical ImageNet training variance. The architectural ideas (retained linear projector, wider last block) are also close to standard projector-based KD practice, limiting novelty.

Presentation issues: Figure 1's subpanel labeling/layout is confusing (panels appear out of order and mislabeled in the rendered figure), and several claims (e.g., 'spectral universality,' 'near-teacher endpoint width/capacity') are stated more strongly than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely important and practically relevant problem: the empirical brittleness of naive feature-map KD when compressing a wide ViT teacher into a much narrower student. The framing of 'per-image low-rank vs. dataset-level wide subspace' is clearly explained and well-illustrated (Figure 1, Table 1).

The cross-architecture/cross-training-regime diagnostics (Table 1 and Appendix B) are systematic and provide a useful empirical survey of SVD vs. shared-PCA effective dimensions across SL/SSL/MM models.

The writing is generally clear and the two proposed remedies (Lift, WideLast) are simple, easy to implement, and reported to improve over the naive baseline on ImageNet-1K. The observation that these changes help even without a teacher (Table 7) is a potentially useful design cue.
Reproducibility signals are reasonable: standard ImageNet-1K protocol, timm teachers, and a claim of released code/data in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: The headline 'paradox' is largely expected rather than surprising. It is close to definitional that per-image SVD rank is far below the shared-subspace PCA dimension for any dataset with diverse inputs; the paper presents a generic property of high-dimensional data as a discovery and labels it 'subspace rotation' without a quantitative rotation measure that goes beyond the SVD/PCA gap.

The SEP analysis—one of the three core contributions—is likely a trivial artifact. A DFT along the channel dimension of a near-white (non-periodic) token vector yields an approximately flat periodogram, so the cumulative SEP is necessarily near-diagonal, exactly as reported. The paper provides no control (e.g., random Gaussian vectors, DCT, or a random orthonormal basis) to show the near-diagonal profile is informative rather than a default property of arbitrary vectors, and the choice of the Fourier basis is unmotivated. Consequently the 'architecture-invariant encoding law' and 'high per-token bandwidth' claims are not established as meaningful capacity measures.

There is a clear gap between the diagnosis and the remedy. The analysis asserts that subspace rotation (input-dependent orientation) is a central failure mode, yet Lift is a fixed linear projector that explicitly cannot adapt to rotation, and the paper concedes it works anyway. This internal tension weakens the causal story that the 'encoding mismatch' explains the failure.

The methods are incremental and their gains are not separated from confounds. WideLast widens the last block to teacher width, adding parameters; the paper does not control for parameter count (e.g., an equal-parameter student with capacity distributed differently), so the improvement may simply reflect added capacity. Both Lift and WideLast essentially amount to providing a wider output layer.

The distillation gains are confounded with standalone gains. Lift/WideLast already improve the non-distilled student (74.86 -> 75.41/75.54), so part of the reported +2.67/+3.37 distillation improvement is attributable to a better base architecture rather than to 'reactivated' feature KD; the paper does not decompose these contributions.

No comparison to existing ViT KD methods. The paper repeatedly claims to 'reactivate feature-map KD' and to clarify 'when and why feature-map KD fails', but it never compares Lift/WideLast against established ViT KD approaches (e.g., ViTKD, ScaleKD, MiniViT, OFA-KD, RSD), nor does it report absolute numbers relative to state-of-the-art compact ViTs. Without this positioning, the significance of the modest gains is unclear.

Statistical rigor is weak. Results appear to be single-seed runs with no error bars, and several key differences (74.86 vs 75.07; 75.46/75.53/75.41/75.23 in Table 4) are within typical run-to-run variance, so conclusions such as 'peaking at 320-dim' and '448-dim hurts' are not supported.

The ablation on feature-loss weight (Table 5) shows small monotone changes (e.g., 76.40 -> 76.74) that again likely fall within noise, and the claim that the goal is to 'match the teacher subspace, not blindly increase dimensionality' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: the reference list contains numerous incorrect years (e.g., ImageNet listed as Deng et al. 2021 while cited as 2009; Hinton et al. 2023 for 2015; Paszke et al. 2024 for 2019; Romero et al. 2021 for 2015; Yim cited as 'Yin et al. 2017'), suggesting insufficient care in preparing the manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practically important problem: feature-map knowledge distillation is often unreliable when compressing a wide ViT teacher into a much narrower student, and the paper attempts to explain why.

The combination of sample-wise SVD, dataset-level PCA, and token-level spectral diagnostics provides a useful multi-view empirical characterization of teacher representations across many architectures, including supervised, self-supervised, and multimodal ViTs.

The proposed remedies (Lift and WideLast) are simple, easy to implement, and show consistent ImageNet-1K improvements over the no-KD baseline. The standalone gains without distillation are interesting and suggest that endpoint design matters beyond KD.

The paper evaluates generality across several teachers (CaiT-S24, DeiT-Small, DeiT3-Small) and includes ablations on head type, projector dimension, and feature-loss weight, which strengthens the empirical picture somewhat.
Code and raw data are stated to be provided in the supplementary materials, and the training protocol is described in enough detail to support reproducibility.
The writing is generally clear, and the motivation for why naive feature matching can fail in wide-to-narrow ViT compression is well articulated.

The SVD/PCA analysis in Table 1 and Appendix B is a useful empirical observation: per-image token matrices can be low-rank while a single shared subspace must be much wider, which is consistent with substantial subspace rotation across inputs.
The paper does not raise apparent ethical concerns and includes a standard impact statement.
weaknesses: A critical control is missing: the paper never reports SoftKD (logit KD) alone for the original unmodified DeiT-Tiny baseline. In Table 3, with Lift, SoftKD alone gives 77.23% while Lift standalone is 75.41%, so logit KD contributes +1.82. Adding feature KD on top of SoftKD gives only +0.27/+0.30. Thus much of the headline gain may come from logit distillation and added capacity rather than from 'reactivating' feature-map KD. The same concern applies to WideLast, where SoftKD alone reaches 77.88% and feature KD adds only +0.28/+0.35.

The capacity interpretation of Lift is questionable. With a standard linear classifier on GAP or [CLS] features, a linear projector 192->384 followed by a linear head 384->1000 is functionally equivalent to a linear head 192->1000. It cannot increase inference-time representational capacity. The standalone Lift gain is therefore more likely an optimization/parameterization effect than evidence of resolving an endpoint bandwidth bottleneck. This undermines a central mechanistic claim.

There are no parameter- or FLOP-matched baselines. WideLast adds a full 384-dimensional Transformer block, substantially increasing parameters and compute. The observed gains could simply come from extra capacity, not specifically from widening the last block. Without comparisons to parameter-matched wider students or alternative capacity placements, the causal claim about endpoint capacity is not established.

The token-level SEP analysis is not well founded. Applying a 1D DFT along the channel dimension assumes a meaningful order or periodicity of channels, but ViT channels are permutation-invariant. A random high-dimensional vector would already produce a roughly diagonal cumulative spectrum, so the 'architecture-invariant encoding law' may be an artifact of using an arbitrary basis rather than a meaningful property of token encodings. A basis-invariant measure such as effective rank or participation ratio would be more appropriate.

The paper infers the proposed mechanism from accuracy alone. It does not directly measure whether Lift or WideLast actually reduce subspace rotation, improve student-teacher feature alignment, or resolve a spectral/bandwidth mismatch. No subspace angles, feature matching metrics, or KD-loss dynamics are reported, so the mechanistic explanation remains correlational.

Dataset-level PCA uses an uncentered second moment. A large mean component across tokens/images could dominate the top principal components and inflate the required shared-subspace dimension. The paper does not discuss how centering or bias terms would affect the 'subspace rotation' conclusion.

The experimental scope is limited: one dataset (ImageNet-1K), one main student (DeiT-Tiny), and one main teacher (CaiT-S24). There are no multiple seeds or error bars, and several reported gains (e.g., +0.21, +0.55, +0.68, +0.27) are small enough that run-to-run variance could matter.

The paper does not compare against state-of-the-art ViT feature KD methods such as ViTKD, ScaleKD, VkD, or RSD, despite citing them. Since the claim is a general fix for feature-map KD, benchmarking against existing solutions is important.

Inference cost is not reported. Lift retains a projector at inference, and WideLast widens the final block; both increase parameters and compute. For a compression setting, accuracy should be compared at matched inference budgets.

Presentation and reference quality need attention: several citations have incorrect years or names (e.g., Deng et al. 2021 for a 2009 paper; Hinton et al. 2023 for 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter 2024 for 2017/2019; 'Yin' instead of 'Yim'), and some figure/formatting artifacts remain.

The limitations discussion is mostly future work rather than an honest treatment of the study's confounds, including the missing SoftKD controls, parameter matching, DFT assumptions, and inference overhead.
